248.t: 101 Ranch and bringing Freddie Keppard's cornet into the district
248.s: Dawson recalls O'Neal Lavasheaux's band, then his own five-piece band at Harry Parker's 101 Ranch and how Keppard got a permit to play cornet.
248.ch: Oliver, Kelly and the district bands
248.q: Well around about 1904 They had O'Neal Lavish there He had a five piece band He was playing at Few Clothes Right on Franklin Near Iberville

248.t: Freddie Keppard and the trumpet at Huntson Nagel's
248.s: The 101 Ranch band was strings only; brass was illegal in the District until Keppard played and Parker got a permit, creating the Magnolia band.
248.ch: Keppard, Oliver and the Magnolia band
248.q: No, that was at the 101 Ranch. We only had string instruments there. And first Minetta was on the piano, then John Bean was on the drum. Old man Bean, Tarcum, on the drum. And I was playing the guitar then. Wasn't I playing? Yeah, I was playing the guitar then. And then we had the old man Willie…

248.t: Playing at Harry Parker's in 1920 with Tinette and Keppard, and the brass ban
248.s: Dawson recounts a small band at Harry Parker's with Manetta, John Vigne and violinist Tinette; brass was banned in the district until Freddie Keppard played a number under Parker's protection.
248.ch: Harry Parker's, the district and its characters
248.q: I was in 19, say 1920, at Fortify. And, uh, Manetto was on the piano and I was playing guitar. John Veen on the drum. And, uh, Tinette on the violin. We didn't have no trumpet, no. I had old man Willie Umprey on the clarinet. Uh-huh. Now, at that time, they didn't allow no, uh, blowing instruments…

771.t: Manuel Perez, Joe Oliver and Freddie Keppard
771.s: He describes Perez as a good reader, recalls first meeting Oliver at Rampart Street, and calls Keppard a gifted but non-reading player.
771.q: Well, he had a little bit of tone, yeah, because he was taught, you know. He was a good teacher, you know. After he knew the fundamentals, you know, up to the horn, you know. Do you remember Joe Oliver? Well Joe come up, just like those other fellas, you know, starting out like that. I remember…

771.t: Joe Oliver, Wooden Joe and loud trumpet playing
771.s: He describes Joe Oliver's style and size, Wooden Joe's local reputation, and how Bolden played improvisation rather than fast fingering.
771.q: Well, Joe was good too. Joe was very good. I played with him a lot too. Well, Joe was powerful. He didn't have too much of a tone, but he was good for jazz because he could make all that, he could make it go like a dog and all that, you understand? You know, that wah-wah stuff and he'd make all…

38.t: Keppard against Oliver: style and rival cliques
38.s: They weigh Keppard against Oliver, noting Keppard's power and that Dreamland was a ballroom while Oliver played cabarets.
38.q: He was powerful. And he had some of Joe's stuff too. Yeah, he had some things just like Joe. Because he, I don't know whether he liked Joe or whether they were jealous or not or not. But he had to admire Joe and he had some of Joe's stuff. As well as everybody else was. Well, you know how you…

38.t: Royal Gardens after Oliver; Cliff King and Freddie Keppard at Harmon's Dreamland
38.s: Wickliffe's band follows Joe Oliver into Royal Gardens around 1926. The next year Levy is with Cliff King at Harmon's Dreamland with Keppard, and King is a showman clarinetist.
38.q: No, I think he was, uh, uh, I think he was playing, don't wait, am I wrong? Was, it was, did he ever play bass? He played bass, sure. Yeah, all right then, all right. I was wondering, I know he played trombone, he played with us too. We went to the, uh, Royal Gardens on 35th Street. You see, Joe…

881.t: Freddie Keppard, early jazz bands and the Chicago split
881.s: Keppard did not record; he recalls the Original Creole Orchestra, Chicago clubs and the Oliver band break-up.
881.q: No, no. Well he might have not wanted to. You know a lot of guys, Freddie Kepa didn't want to record. A lot of guys didn't want to record. You see a lot of guys didn't want to record.

881.t: Freddie Keppard's power and Joe Oliver's mute effects
881.s: Keppard blasted the big Dreamland band, while Oliver used big hands and mutes for effects like the baby cry on Eccentric.
881.ch: Oliver's circle and old New Orleans players
881.q: Oh yeah, he's about the strongest of all the fellas. Joe Oliver was strong. But you see Joe Oliver, he did a whole lot of playing mutes. Joe Oliver had large hands. And at that time the mute that he was using was just about this long. You see his hand was covered in mute. And he had all kinds of…

300.t: What made Petit's band popular; Freddie Keppard
300.s: He says Petit's band was together with good rhythm and he only just missed hearing Keppard in Chicago.
300.q: Well they just naturally had a good band. They was together. They had wonderful trombone player. Zebra Norris was good. Good rhythm. Buddy was a good trumpet.

300.s: Humphrey says the trumpeter was good, between Armstrong and Bunk Johnson in some phrases, with ideas of his own.
300.q: Well, it's hard to describe. He'd probably, mostly have to hear the fellow's play. That's right. I'm afraid we won't be able to do that album. He played on a difference between, well, between Lewis Armstrong and, of course, the old-time great. and,

768.t: Freddie Keppard's playing compared with Oliver's organized band
768.s: She played with Keppard at the Deluxe and Lorraine Gardens, thought him a fine trumpeter, and contrasts the unarranged work with Oliver's well-organized band.
768.q: Well, I told you he played a short time of Deluxe with us when Sugar Johnny was taking L. And then I doubled with Freddie Kepard out of Lorraine Gardens. That was, must have been 40th and stayed out that way somewhere. That was an after-hour place. I played with him there. I think he was a very…

253.t: Comparing Joe Oliver, Chris Kelly and Kid Rena to Petit
253.s: Hall compares Oliver, Chris Kelly, Kid Rena and Armstrong as players, saying Petit knew his instrument best.
253.q: Well, Oliver, well I didn't know too much, I didn't know too much about Joe Oliver. I didn't know too much, I heard him several times because he came out the reserve when I was a kid and played Kid Ory, Oliver, Baby Dots, Johnny Dots, and that bunch, you know, I heard him. But, by the pity, I…

1000.t: Joe Oliver's mutes, Kid Ory, and Freddie Keppard
1000.s: Discussion of Oliver's mutes (confused with Ory on trombone) and a single memory of Freddie Keppard at Perseverance Hall.
1000.q: Yeah, Freddie Keppert, I remember him. The last time I seen him, the last time I seen Freddie Keppert was around at the Corporator's Hall. That was the last job I seen him play. I never heard no more of him. Freddie Keppert went left here or something. I don't know what happened to Freddie Keppert.…

252.t: Freddie Keppard, known only by reputation
252.s: She knew of Keppard as a good cornet player around Chicago but not personally.
252.q: Freddie? Freddie Kepler. Well, I didn't know of any band he had. I just know that he played good connect, and I know he used to play around Chicago. Oh, yeah. Uh-huh.

568.t: Freddie Keppard's refusal to record and the Scissor Grinder
568.s: Hightower compares his own guarded playing to Keppard, who recorded only one number, 'Scissor Grinder', fearing others would steal his ideas.
568.q: Yeah, we got all the greatest bands you want to hear. That was a really a good band. They were really great. And we got along pretty good, but most of those fellows, as we will get back to myself about recording and numbers recording, I'm something like Freddie Kepler was if you never heard about…

36.t: Comparing Keppard, Oliver and Bunk Johnson
36.s: Simeon played with Keppard at the Savoy under Charlie Elgar; Keppard had more drive and a bigger tone than Oliver, while Bunk was creative but more subdued.
36.q: Yeah, I played with Keppard for a while. How did you like him? At the Svobal with Charlie Elgin. Oh, he was a terrific drive, a trumpet player. He was a nice tone.

907.s: He knows Natty Dominique and played a small job with Freddie Keppard.
907.q: a small job a full piece artist right down there I forget I think they called it Funky London during that time excuse the expression what we was playing in there making the money on those kind of things or Joe Oliver

46.s: He calls Keppard among the greatest, playing ragtime, which was all Scott Joplin before it was called jazz.
46.ch: Hightower: New Orleans parades and early players
46.q: Yeah, that's what they used to advertise. Yeah, that's right. In a puncture wagon, horse and wagon. And he never was no more good. He'd take him sick and they'd take him to the hospital. There was no good. And shortly after that, he died. But I didn't realize, but they said, after Freddie come up…

866.t: Hearing George Baquet with Freddie Keppard
866.s: Angrum never heard McCurdy play. He listened to George Baquet in Freddie Keppard's band, praising his low register, and describes Keppard as a big, powerful trumpeter.
866.q: Yeah, I haven't heard of Barquet. Barquet used to play with Freddie Kepler. Used to play with Freddie Kepler lots of time. I used to go to dancing. George Barquet was playing. I had to sit right up under the music stand, listen to that man play, crying there. Was he good? He was real good. Right.…

48.s: Keppard played with Palmer's band at Dreamland; his style, sweating, compared with Armstrong.
48.q: Did you play with him? He played with him. He played, he come with us at Deluxe. At not Deluxe, at Dream. And he played with us a while at Dream. That was a Dream one at 35th Street and State.

5.t: Freddie Keppard, Oliver and Armstrong compared
5.s: He swaps places with Keppard in Cook's band and judges Keppard strong but below Armstrong and Oliver; Armstrong had better technique, Oliver better ideas.
5.q: Uh, at the White, at White City. Yeah. And he, uh, he was with him over to Dreamland too. He, he came in after I did. He'd take my place over to Dreamland. Yeah. And I'd take his place at, uh, White City. Uh huh. So, uh, I worked with Charlie Cook. Charlie Cook. Charlie Cook. I think Charlie, I…

127.t: Hearing Keppard, Bunk Johnson and Bolden
127.s: He met Freddie Keppard in Chicago, heard Bunk on a Homer excursion, and never heard Bolden.
127.q: Well, yes. I'll tell you how I heard bunk. I was in the country, and the excursion was going from New Orleans to Homer, Louisiana, and I caught the excursion at a race, and they went to Homer and stood right by him all day, listening to them blokes. That's how I met him.

290.t: Louis Cottrell, the Magnolia Band, Freddie Keppard and popularity
290.s: He played occasionally with Louis Cottrell and admired Freddie Keppard, popular in the Olympia band.
290.q: I knew of the Magnolia Band. I know Louis Caput was with him, I thought maybe that was the same. You didn't know Caput's brother. Freddie? Yeah. I knew him like this, to the public. You never met him. No. Somebody say that's Freddie Caput. And then I'd see him on different occasions and I'd…

55.s: Keppard's style, the Original Creole circus tour, and him being more of a musician than Bolden.
55.q: Oh sure. He knew him. Freddie Kepard, they're talking about jazz in New Orleans. Freddie Kepard. Big guy Louie, called Louie Nelson.

690.t: New Orleans cornetists: Perez, Oliver, Keppard
690.s: Pope remembers Manuel Perez and Joe Oliver visiting Mobile but not Keppard or Bolden.
690.q: Did you ever hear him? I don't remember him, but I do remember Emmanuel Teres. Oh, yes. Do you remember him? Yes, I met him. I knew him. He died too. I didn't hear him play. Yeah, right. He always compared me with Perry. He used to come over here. Yeah, he did. I used to show off a little bit, you…

650.t: Joe Oliver, Freddie Keppard and other trumpeters compared
650.s: He says Oliver made Louis Armstrong but rates Freddie Keppard as good or better, and comments on Baquet, Perez and Louis's lasting success.
650.q: Oh, I pushed a friend of mine. He's the one that made Louis. I guess you know that, don't you? Yeah, he made Louis. And Louis admits that too. He made Louis. That's a lovely player too, Joe Oliver was. He used to call him King Oliver, you know. But I never thought, I never see Joe in that light of…

56.s: Ory liked Keppard's band best; Keppard was powerful, never used mute and had gone before Oliver rose.
56.q: Yeah. Then Freddie had, Freddie was very powerful, you know, trumpet player. He really played lots of trumpet down there.

801.t: John leaves with Armstrong; Freddie Keppard
801.s: Eddie recalls John leaving for Chicago when Joe Oliver sent for Louis, then praises a cornetist's high-register playing.
801.q: Well you see, yeah he played the guitar banjo. He never played a tenor banjo. He played the guitar banjo, the six string banjo. He still does. He still play that. Yeah. I remember when he left here with Louis Armstrong in there. Yeah, went to Chicago, that's right.

15.t: Freddie Keppard at the Deluxe: his tone, fear of recording and gin
15.s: Howard played with Keppard, praising his sweet tone, noting his fear of having his stuff stolen on records, and describing his heavy gin habit.
15.ch: Chicago in the 1920s: Bix, Armstrong, Morton
15.q: Sure. Did you play with Cap? Heck yes. Where? At the Deluxe. Oh you did? Sure did. How was he as a trumpet player? Marvelous. Marvelous. Sweet tone and a hell of a lip. Oh yeah? Yes. It's too bad he didn't make any records to my big thing. He had a complex about his records. Somebody wanted to make…

23.t: Joe Oliver blowing outside against Freddie Keppard
23.s: Rose confirms the story of Oliver walking out and blowing a B-flat blues with Richard M. Jones at the piano to draw the crowd from Keppard's club. He then turns to the Albert system clarinet.
23.ch: New Orleans bands, Oliver and Armstrong
23.q: Well, it's an absolutely accurate story. No question that, that it, that it took place. No, he did this by himself. Did this by himself. Not,

783.t: Freddie Keppard compared with Joe Oliver
783.s: Shoffner says Keppard was a faster reader than Oliver, rougher and stronger with a different style, and used an open horn where Oliver used mutes.
783.q: Yeah, he was a much faster reader than Joe Oliver, you see. But he had a different style altogether. His style was, well, you couldn't compare the two, because he had a different style.

25.t: Freddie Keppard's style, New York trip and recording
25.s: He recalls Keppard's loud outside-man playing, the Coconut Grove job, drinking habits, reading ability and the head arrangements on the record.
25.q: But, yes, Freddie Kepard was a great outside man, we would call him. I know that the story of him, Tim Brim in New York, that the Coconut Grove had a band, a great band over there, something like 15 pieces. And he wanted, he kept hearing about this New Orleans style of music. So Freddie Kepard told…

400.s: Hinton remembers Keppard as a powerhouse trumpeter, older and ill when they played at a Bingham State Bank ballroom at 35th and State.
400.ch: Eddie South, high school and the South Side scene
400.q: He was older and he was getting sick. He lived right near me, 35th and State Street, just… Bingham… [unintelligible] had a bank, Bingham State Bank. He‟d opened a new building, a new office building at 35th and State and they had a ballroom there and he got the job as a bandleader.

1.t: Freddie Keppard: loud ragtime trumpet and the Orpheum circuit
1.s: Danny and Milt recall Keppard's loud, ragged style and his decade on the Orpheum circuit with the Original Dixieland band.
1.ch: Wagon bands, halls and the old brass bands
1.q: Well, he had been on the Orpheum circuit for about ten years, from about 1909, the year I was born, until, what, 1918 or 1919, when the Dixieland Band recorded... Them people had been on the Orpheum circuit, him and Big-Eye Louis, a band from New Orleans...

67.t: Freddie Keppard's handkerchief over his valves
67.s: Keppard hid his fingering from copyists and once blew a mute across a club floor; Cheatham found him loud and crude but good.
67.q: That's a true story. One day in Chicago, the word got out that Freddy Kephard played -- was playing and he blew a note so loud that he -- that the straight mute that he was playing jumped clean out of his horn, went all away across the night club floor. He hit this note, and so naturally everybody…

106.t: Freddie Keppard's tin cans, flutter-tongue and technique
106.s: Briggs describes Keppard as a technical freak player with tin-can effects, flutter-tongue, half-valves, a sharp attack and fast technique, and notes how high trumpet ranges were regarded then.
106.ch: Will Marion Cook and the Southern Syncopated Orchestra
106.q: Keppard, I think that he was curious. He invented, more or less, the system of using tin cans and that sort of thing on his bell, to get different sounds, you see.

29.t: The Keppard band played soft as well as loud
29.s: From the article, Howard confirms that the Keppard musicians did not play loud, rehearsed with a keg of beer, and played real music.
29.q: That's right. No, they didn't; they didn't play loud; they wan't loud players.

72.t: What Oliver said of New Orleans: Keppard and Bolden
72.s: Oliver talked mainly about Freddie Keppard and admired Buddy Bolden's style.
72.q: Yeah. A trumpet player. He used to talk about him all the time. Otherwise, he'd... He liked Freddie Keppard's playing very much, more than anybody in New Orleans. He didn't speak too much about Bunk Johnson.

8.s: Garland describes 'Chork' Oliver's bad eye and wa-wa sounds made with a glass, derby and coffee can, and his hot, powerful playing.
8.q: He was a hot player, yes. (Held make all them funny things on his horn, unintelligible.)

77.t: Freddie Keppard with his handkerchief, Jimmy Noone and King Oliver's soft playing
77.s: Keppard covered his horn with a handkerchief and was powerful; Lil thought him better than Oliver; Hunter knew him little.
77.q: Always. Always. That's right. That's right. He covered his horn with a handkerchief all the time. He sure did. And he -- well, I won't say that because I want to tell about Joe Oliver, how soft he would play. But Freddie Keppard, oh, he was a marvelous trumpet player. You called them trumpets then,…

13.t: Freddie Keppard, Sidney Bechet and the Villa Venice band
13.s: Wilson recalls a reading band at a gangster road house with Keppard, Bechet and Darnell Howard, and Keppard's power and secrecy.
13.q: It was Shepperd -- what's his name, Freddie Keppard, Darnell Howard on saxophone, Bushell on saxophone, and who the heck was on trombone? Fellow by the name of Burt -- Burt something. Used to have a club at the Musicians Union. He played trombone. But the name I remember is Darnell Howard and…
